extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students and researchers in journalism/media studies and linguistics studying news values, news selection, and news photography
extracted.subtask_description: A cross-disciplinary working-paper survey of how 'news values' (newsworthiness criteria) have been conceptualized, measured and applied across Media/Journalism Studies and Linguistics, including text and visual (photographic) criteria. It summarizes classic lists (e.g. Galtung & Ruge), subsequent revisions, critiques, and methodological implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Galtung & Ruge's news factors: the time-span needed for the event to unfold; the more similar the frequency of the event is to the frequency of the news medium, the more probable it will be recorded as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in hypotheses about news selection; related to news cycle and medium (e.g. daily vs. continuous coverage). Hoskins & O’Loughlin argue television mediatises time, affecting frequency's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold (absolute intensity, intensity increase)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: events that exceed a certain intensity or show a marked change in intensity are more likely to be newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalised in some content analyses as degree/magnitude of event impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: events with a clear, unambiguous interpretation are preferred; the less ambiguity, the more likely an event will be noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects to news writing objectives (clarity, simplification); content analyses often code for clarity/interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness (cultural proximity, relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: the extent to which an event has cultural proximity or relevance to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also discussed as 'proximity' in later taxonomies (geographical, cultural, psychological).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance (predictability, demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: events that fit pre-existing themes, expectations or patterns are more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to editorial routines, news agenda and the desire for thematic fit with other items (composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness (unpredictability, scarcity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: events that are novel, surprising, or scarce tend to be more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often operationalised as 'novelty' or 'surprise' in later taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: once an event is in the news it tends to stay in the news; the unfolding of a story over time increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to follow-up and the news cycle; used to explain persistence of story coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition (fit with other news items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: how an item fits with the mix of other items selected; editors strive for a balanced whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain editorial packaging, placement decisions and story mixture on pages/bulletins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor (culture-bound): events involving elite nations are more likely to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of prominence/eliteness cluster; often coded in content analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite people
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor (culture-bound): events involving elite or high-status people increase newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently labelled Prominence, Celebrity, Power, Worth in later lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: the presence of identifiable persons (vs. abstract processes) increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to personalization and human-interest values (concretizing issues via people).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to something negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge factor: negative events (damage, disruption, destruction) are more likely to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to 'negativity', 'conflict', 'bad news' in many later taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge hypothesis: the higher the total score of an event across factors, the higher the probability it will become news and make headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied scoring model for aggregating news factors; not fully tested by Galtung & Ruge but influential in quantitative approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Galtung & Ruge hypothesis: an event low on one news factor must be high on another complementary factor to make the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify multi-dimensional measurement of newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power elite / Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Harcup & O’Neill / Masterton / others: the presence or involvement of powerful or prominent people increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears under many labels (Eliteness, Celebrity, Status); examples and definitions across multiple researchers are very similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving celebrities (A-list people, royalty, TV stars) are judged newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often combines with picture opportunities and entertainment values to strongly drive coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment / Picture opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Harcup & O’Neill and others: entertainment value (including picture opportunities) can lead to inclusion even when intrinsic newsworthiness is low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a good photograph or cuddly animal plus celebrity can be irresistible to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise / Unexpectedness (Harcup & O’Neill label)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that surprise readers or deviate from expectations are more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlaps with Galtung & Ruge's Unexpectedness / Novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news / Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Harcup & O’Neill identify 'bad news' as a criterion — negative developments (damage, injury, scandal) attract coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely associated with 'conflict' and 'negativity' in photographic analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news / Positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some taxonomies include 'good news' as a separate value — positive developments may be represented visually or as feature items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be used to provide balance or human-interest counterpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Impact / Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The bigger the impact or consequences of an event, the greater its newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in some studies by scale, placement, length of coverage; applied to both text and images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance / Worth
rubrics_metrics.description: A story's relevance to the audience or perceived worthiness shapes selection (Brighton & Foy: Relevance/Worth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tied to audience-orientation approaches (e.g. Guo 2012: 'value materialised when read').

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that allow for subsequent reporting or ongoing development are more likely to be maintained in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to continuity and the news cycle; measured as 'follow-up' in content analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper/Organisational agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that fit the news organisation's own agenda or thematic priorities are selected or given prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why similar events might be covered differently across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest (Masterton core value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterton: core value meaning the story must be interesting to be news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of Masterton's three core values (with Timeliness and Clarity) claimed to be globally accepted by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterton core value and widespread criterion: recency of event increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical in broadcast and press; relates to frequency and the news cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterton core value: the story should be clear and comprehensible on its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tied to news writing objectives such as Unambiguity and Simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterton: the consequence or significance of an event for the audience is a news criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synonymous with Impact/Magnitude/Significance in many lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterton and others: geographical, cultural or psychological nearness to the audience increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often operationalised in local vs. national vs. international coding schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterton and many others: conflict/drama/controversy are strong drivers of news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominent in both text and photographic news value lists (conflict images are high in news photos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest / Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that humanise issues, provide emotional connection or personalize events increase newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely tied to personalization, emotions, and picture-based storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Newness or internal novelty (news peg) makes a story more likely to be considered newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the 'novelty/unexpectedness' cluster and linked to editors' avoidance of 'stale' content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency / Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Conley & Lamble / Brighton & Foy: stories that are topical or currently in public discussion (currency) have news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to timeliness and news agenda; Brighton & Foy emphasise digital-age topicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on audience retention (Eilders' relevance schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eilders: news factors establish a relevance schema that guides selective attention and retention in audiences; journalists' perceptions of these factors are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies evaluation should consider audience cognitive schemas and what drives recall/retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance (Shoemaker et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an event deviates from social norms; more deviant events predicted to receive more prominent coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured on scales in empirical studies (e.g. four-point deviance scales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Status / Identification (Schulz higher-order dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schulz dimensions include status, valence, relevance, identification, consonance and dynamics as organizational criteria of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalised via frequency, position, length and presentation in content analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: A news-writing objective and Østgaard internal factor: simplifying complex events to make them understandable increases likelihood of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains preference for concrete/personalized stories over abstract/process-driven items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: A news-writing objective: concise, 'closely packed' stories are preferred, especially important for broadcast where time/space is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affects selection and story construction (editing for space/time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presupposition / Backgrounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing necessary background or summarising presupposed information makes stories more intelligible and thus more publishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A news-writing guideline; influences how topics are framed and whether they are acceptable for audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (news-writing objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing the story so it can be understood by readers/viewers is a core objective guiding news construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces Masterton's 'Clarity' core value; used as a coding/quality criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story quality / Aesthetic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements such as action, pace, completeness, and technical/aesthetic features may be considered when judging or selecting stories (esp. features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly relevant for feature journalism and award-winning photography.

rubrics_metrics.name: News barrier (Østgaard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of internal factors that make news 'palatable' and determine whether news flows; includes simplicity, identification and other gatekeeping constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why some events never pass into news circulation despite potential relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisational / Commercial pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Budget, market orientation, audience type, competition and editorial priorities influence selection independent of event attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classified by some researchers as selection factors rather than news values per se, but crucial to any meaningful analysis of newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: External influences (Brighton & Foy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors outside journalistic practice (owners, advertisers, politicians, PR) that can 'corrupt' or shape news selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton & Foy include this as a 'new news value' to capture 21st-century pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gans' external enduring values (ethnocentrism, altruistic democracy, responsible capitalism, small-town pastoralism, individualism, moderatism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gans identifies a set of enduring societal values that inform selection and how actors/activities are reported or ignored (e.g., ethnocentrism, individualism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain ideological patterns in selection beyond event-level factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture opportunity / Visual attractiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: In visual news, the availability of original pictures or film and the dramatic/attractive qualities of imagery increase likelihood of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harcup & O’Neill note that good pictures can secure coverage even when intrinsic newsworthiness is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution and photographic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographic quality (colour, contrast, light, perspective, dramatic effort) contributes to visual news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant when assessing award-winning press photography and editorial photo selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / Consequence (visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: News photographs are judged on the significance or immediate interest of the depicted event; local spot news often dominates award-winning photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links photographic choices to impact on local audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict / Dramatization (visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images showing conflict, damage, violence or controversy are highly newsworthy in visual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many press photos embody tension and conflict; however, most press photos also show aftermath rather than live drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity (visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive or human-interest images may be used to entertain or balance 'hard' news stories and are more likely in feature photo slots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual representation can serve realist/objective or diversionary/entertainment functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: For news photos, recency is crucial; news photos typically depict ephemeral situations (floods, shootings) rather than lingering feature topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness distinguishes news photography from feature imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization / Emotions (visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photos that concretize issues through people, depict emotions, or personalize events enhance identification and news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization helps audiences identify with stories; images often foreground working/middle-class people rather than elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality / Eroticism (visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual or erotic imagery can function as a distinct visual news value in selection decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in photographic taxonomies as an occasional factor driving selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition (visual balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors consider how a photograph fits within the broader mix of images and stories to achieve balance on a page or bulletin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to textual composition; affects placement and pairing with stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of visualization / Ready-made text
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of ready-made material (photos, video or press releases) that journalists can re-use increases the likelihood of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linked to prefabrication, deadlines and pressures of the news cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefabrication / Follow-through (news-cycle production factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of prescheduled or ready-to-run material improves chances of coverage; once in the news, stories are easier to follow up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains editorial choices under deadline and resource constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' perceptions / Cognitive internalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The cognitive perspective: news values are internalised professional criteria or 'journalistic hypotheses' guiding selective attention and decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies methods should consider interviews, observation and ethnography (not only content analysis) to capture these perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discursive construction of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: A discursive perspective: newsworthiness is constructed through language, photography and production texts that build the sense of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages analysis of how texts and visuals perform news-value construction, not just whether factors are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological recommendation: multi-method approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers (e.g., Staab) recommend combining content analysis, surveys of journalists and newsroom observation to study news factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges limitations of single-method designs (e.g., content analysis alone cannot explain why a story was selected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection factors vs. news values distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Bednarek & Caple propose distinguishing (a) news writing objectives (clarity, brevity, colour), (b) selection factors (any criterion affecting whether something is published, including commercial pressures), and (c) news values (newsworthiness proper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite framing to avoid conflating organisational/market factors with intrinsic newsworthiness.
